evidence.note: The Public Domain Review says D.O.A. is in the US public domain 'due to an error related to the renewal of the copyright.' This is a secondary source. I could not open the Catalog of Copyright Entries renewal volumes or the Copyright Office public catalog to confirm that no renewal exists, so the print is not marked verified_pd.
I did not check who composed the score or whether the music was separately registered or renewed. A sound film's recorded track normally shares the film's own status, but this is unconfirmed here.
I did not confirm the screenplay credits or whether the film was based on an earlier published work, so the story layer is unresolved.

editorial:
D.O.A. is a 1950 film noir directed by Rudolph Maté, who had been nominated for the Academy Award for Best Cinematography five years in a row in the 1940s. A poisoned man walks into a police station to report his own murder, then spends the rest of the film finding out who did it. Creators reuse it for clips, remixes and noir-themed edits.

The Public Domain Review says the film is in the US public domain because of an error in renewing its copyright. That is a secondary claim. This dossier could not check the renewal records themselves, so the print stays undetermined until someone searches the Copyright Office catalog and the Stanford renewal database. The rights trap is the layers beyond the picture. The music and the underlying screenplay were not checked and may carry their own registrations. Any restored or re-scored release may also add protected material. Check each of those before commercial reuse.
faq: The Public Domain Review says its copyright lapsed through a renewal error. This dossier could not confirm that in the primary renewal records, so search the Stanford renewal database and the Copyright Office catalog yourself before relying on it. The music, the story and any modern restoration should be checked separately.
Where can I watch or download a copy?

The Internet Archive has an item at https://archive.org/details/DOA1950. It is a community upload, and its metadata confirms the title and year. The source and quality of that print were not verified. A restored release may include added material, such as new titles or a new score, that is protected separately.
